title: The moon's two halves
hookLine: the moon cursed to waste away and given back half of every month; why Hindu holy days move with it
carry: holy days follow the moon, and come round again

cards: Here's a question Hindu kids get asked at school every year: why is Diwali on a different date this time?

Holi, Janmashtami, Ganesh Chaturthi, nearly every festival of the last two and a half weeks wanders around the wall calendar. The answer is the moon. And Hindus tell a story about why the moon grows and shrinks at all.

teach.b: The sage Daksha had many daughters, and twenty-seven of them married the Moon, Chandra. Each wife was a star, one of the twenty-seven the moon passes through each month.
But Chandra loved only Rohini, and spent every night with her. The others went home to their father in tears. Daksha warned him: treat them all alike.
Chandra didn't change, so Daksha cursed him to waste away. Night by night the moon grew thinner, and the plants he cared for began to fail.

teach.h: A CURSE, SOFTENED: HALF DARK, HALF BRIGHT.
teach.b: In one well-loved telling, Chandra went to the shore at Prabhasa, in Gujarat, and prayed to Shiva, and Shiva softened the curse: the moon would fade for half of every month and grow back for the other half.
Pilgrims still go to the temple there, Somnath, lord of the moon. Here's what that means at home.
A Hindu month really is counted in those two halves: the bright half, as the moon grows, and the dark half, as it shrinks. Each lunar day is a tithi. Diwali falls on a new moon.
Ganesh Chaturthi, on the fourth day of the bright half. So the festivals ride the moon and drift across a sun calendar.
To find them, families use a panchang, an almanac of five limbs: the lunar day, the weekday, the star the moon is passing, and two more ways of dividing time.

teach.h: THE HOLY DAYS COME ROUND AGAIN.
teach.b: And because the moon always comes back, so do the holy days. Nobody keeps them all; families keep what their region and parents keep. Missed one this year?
The moon is already on its way round.

how: Most Hindu festivals are set by a lunar day, a tithi, in the bright or dark half of a lunar month, so families find each year's dates in a panchang, a printed almanac or app; the waxing and waning moon is told in the story of Daksha's curse on Chandra, softened by Shiva at Prabhasa (Somnath).

the almanac that gives each day's lunar date

games.q: the moon and the calendar — tap the pairs.
p: the star-wife the moon loved most

s: in the story, Shiva lifts Daksha's curse completely
he softens it: the moon fades for half the month and grows back for the other half.
Hindu festival dates move because they follow the moon
each is set by a lunar day, a tithi, so the wall-calendar date shifts.
if you miss a festival, it's gone for good
the moon comes round, and so do the holy days. nobody keeps them all.

games.q: you missed Navaratri this year: exams, no time. what does the moon's story teach?
o: it's gone. you missed your chance.
the holy days come round with the moon. keep it next year.
do all nine nights tomorrow to catch up.
games.why: the moon wanes and comes back, and Hindu holy days come round with it. the calendar itself gives you another turn.

practice: Tonight, if you can, find the moon. Is it growing or shrinking: the bright half, or the dark? On some fast nights, many Hindus offer a little water toward the rising moon before they eat.
If you pray, fold your hands and greet it; if you don't, just look. Then name one festival you'd like to keep this coming year, and say it to the moon: see you when you come round again.

wordCard.voice: Panchang. The Hindu almanac of five limbs, the lunar day, the weekday, the moon's star and two more, so families know when the holy days come round.

sources.ref: Chandra, Daksha's daughters and the curse; healed at Prabhasa (Mahabharata, Shalya Parva)
Somnath: Chandra worships Shiva at Prabhasa, who sets the waxing and waning halves (Shiva Purana, Kotirudra Samhita)
The Hindu lunisolar calendar: tithi, paksha, adhika masa; the panchanga's five limbs
